Mr. Speaker, yesterday the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre asked the following question:
By what date are employers required to furnish T-4 slips to their employees, and what penalty is there in the case of any employer who does not meet the deadline?
Under section 209 of the income tax regulations every person required to file a return referred to in section 200 of the regulations shall forward to each taxpayer, in respect of whose income the return relates, two copies of the portion of the return relating to such taxpayer by the last day of February following the end of the calendar year in which the income was earned. subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO ACT EXTENDING APPLICATION, FIXING INTEREST AND INCREASING MAXIMUM

speechtext:
The house resumed, from Wednesday, March 13, consideration in committee of the following resolution-Mr. Howe (Port Arthur)-Mr. Robinson (Simcoe East) in the chair:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Prairie Grain Producers Interim Financing Act, 1956 to enable the governor in council to extend the application of the act to authorize and govern guaranteed loans that may be made by banks in the period September 1, 1957 to June 1, 1958; to provide that the rate of interest charged by the banks on a loan shall not exceed a rate prescribed by the governor in council; and to increase the maximum amount of a loan from fifteen hundred dollars to three thousand dollars.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO ACT EXTENDING APPLICATION, FIXING INTEREST AND INCREASING MAXIMUM
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the
amendments that are provided for in the resolution now before this committee were set forth yesterday by the Minister of Trade and Commerce in these words as reported at page 2161 of Hansard:
.	.	. that the maximum amount of loan to an
individual producer be raised from $1,500 to $3,000; second, that the rate of interest, which is 5 per cent at present, be left to the determination of the governor in council; and loans be extended by one month by moving the opening date forward from October 1 to September 1.
That in general represents the changes that are to be made when the bill is brought before the house. I believe that what is being done here represents a complete disregard of the wishes and requirements of all western farm organizations and of farmers throughout western Canada.
I am not going to refer to the several resolutions that have been passed by western farm organizations, because they have already been placed on the record and need not be repeated. However, I summarize them in effect by saying that all farm organizations in the prairie provinces have demanded cash advances, that in no case has there been the acceptance in whole or in part of a system such as is contemplated by this resolution, which continues the legislation passed last year.
The general attitude taken by farmers everywhere is that because of the fact that the wheat board is the sole purchaser of their wheat, the inability to market it is not their responsibility and therefore there is no reason why they should be denied their cash

advances as asked for. They deny particularly and categorically that they should be required to pay interest on what in effect is their income for the current year.
For several years we in this party have been supporting the need for cash advances. In 1952, as reported in Hansard for December 17 of that year, Hon. George Drew, then leader of the opposition, supported an amendment which had been moved recommending legislation providing for the payment to producers in respect of farm-stored grain of an advance equal to 75 per cent of the initial price established at August 1 in each crop year. Our only change over the passing years has been that while 75 per cent was the amount asked for at that time, the demand since has been generally that 50 per cent should be advanced. That demand has been universal, and in the face of that demand the bringing in of a loan system again is a denial of the wishes of farmers everywhere.
The last example, an epitome of the demands of farmers, was brought to the attention of the cabinet and members in all parts of this house by the council of farm unions, who demanded that as a matter of policy that cash advances be provided for. Two or three weeks ago when I was in Prince Albert I met with representatives of labour and agriculture.
The major demand made by them was that such a system should be brought into effect. It is recommended by the Gordon commission; it is demanded by various farm organizations other than the farm union; it is something which can be brought into effect without the possibility of loss, for there is only one market in which the farmer can sell his wheat. Last year when the matter was before the house we pointed out the general situation and the demand that had been made, and as far as I am concerned I am not going to repeat the arguments then advanced.
I summarize our attitude toward this resolution and the bill to be founded thereon as follows. What is being given to the farmer is a stone when he is asking for bread, and what is being provided under this resolution is something unwanted by the farmer, something totally ineffective to meet his needs, and something which in effect will be inoperative, as was the legislation to a large extent during the past year.
Last year when we discussed this matter there were all manner of excuses advanced by the minister as to why cash advances should not be substituted in favour of this general plan of farm loans upon which the farmer will pay interest. One of the major objections was that if such a plan were brought into

effect the members of the wheat board would resign. That was the answer given by the minister; that was the basic reason given why the general demand of the farmers could not be met. In the light of answers given subsequently to questions asked, that alibi of the Minister of Trade and Commerce has been proved to be without foundation. When that statement was made by the minister hon. members of this house actually concluded that the minister had been in communication with members of the wheat board. As reported on page 992 of Hansard for February 8. 1956, I asked this question:
1.	Did the chairman or any members of the wheat board notify the government at any time since July 1, 1955, that they would resign within a matter of days if loans on farm-stored wheat were brought into effect? If so, which of them did so?
That question embodied the statement that had been made by the minister. My question continued:
2.	What was the date or dates of said notifications and were same given verbally or in writing?
The answer by the Minister of Trade and Commerce was as follows:
1.	No.
2.	Answered by 1 above.
Then to overcome the possibility that some time the minister might say that question did not cover the statement he had made I asked a further question, as reported at page 1096 of Hansard for February 10, 1956, as follows:
1. Did the chairman or any members of the wheat board notify the government at any time since July 1, 1955, that they would resign within a matter of days if cash advances on farm-stored wheat were brought into effect?
The minister answered that question with a categorical "No". In other words, the basis of the opposition last year by the minister was that the wheat board would resign. There was no ground for that statement; it was a meaningless evasion of the situation and a denial of the demands of the farmers by an excuse which in the light of questions subsequently asked was proved to be entirely incorrect.
I have said before that the farmer demands action in this regard. The situation today in western Canada is that on every hand the farmers are pleading for cash.
In many parts they are unable to market their wheat. I do not have the exact figures available, but at approximately one-third of the marketing points the quota is 2 bushels an acre. Last year the farmers were promised that in those areas that had suffered discrimination in 1955-56 the situation would be remedied and larger quotas would be made available. In many cases such is not the fact.
Grain
The first argument was that the wheat board would resign if cash advances were instituted. That was not true. The second argument was that there was a possible danger of loss. That argument is totally ineffectual, for the reason that there is no quota except for recognized farmers and each farmer has his quota book. The third argument was that it was not generally demanded. That argument was refuted at the time by bringing to the attention of the committee and the house resolutions passed in every part of western Canada.
The same situation prevails today. Without exception among the wheat pools, among the farmers' unions, among the members of the federation of agriculture, what they demand is cash advances. Here the farmers find themselves once more handed a proposition requiring them to pay interest on their earnings. I should like to know what would happen in this country if the government were unable to dispose of the product of the people who labour to produce it and were therefore unable to pay them their just due. What would happen if these people, in place of the payment to which they were entitled, were given the opportunity to go to the bank, get an advance and pay interest on what they had rightfully earned?
In addition to the general objection, there is also the further objection this year that instead of the interest rate being properly placed before the house and the country it is left with the uncertainty of fixation at some time in the future. While I realize that interest rates in general have been rising by reason of the actions of the government, nonetheless there can be no justification for any additional interest rate being paid by farmers on such advances. There was no justification for interest being paid in the first place, and there is no justification for an additional amount being paid.
Those in general summarize the arguments that we in this party have advanced through the hon. member for Calgary North and the hon. member for Brandon-Souris. They represent the stand we have taken since 1952. We believe that the only salvation for the western farmer, with his markets lost and his wheat therefore unmarketable, is that there should be cash advances. Second, we believe that every encouragement should be given to the farmer to provide his own storage, and that in the provision of such storage additional write-offs should be permitted when determining the amount of his income tax. We believe that under proper circumstances there should be provision for cash advances on farm-stored grain similar to the system in effect in the United States.

Grain
Those in general represent the stands taken by the official opposition. Repeating those stands is entirely unnecessary. Summarized, our attitude is that this is another makeshift, another postponement of effective action. This is another delaying action. The farmers today are asking for justice. They are not asking for measures such as this, which simply postpone the day when effective action must and will be taken.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO ACT EXTENDING APPLICATION, FIXING INTEREST AND INCREASING MAXIMUM
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am sure that members who are concerned with the wheat economy of Canada are greatly disappointed that this legislation is the best the Minister of Trade and Commerce can present to the parliament of Canada at this time. Although there are about 200,000 wheat farmers interested in the legislation, the minister stated yesterday that limited use has been made of the facilities available under the act. The hon. member for Kindersley pointed out that the maximum number was 15,370. That is well below 10 per cent of the people in the area.
A year ago when we were discussing this matter members who were opposing the legislation stated that the fact that very few people would go to the banks to borrow money on their own grain would not indicate that the farmers involved were not in very difficult circumstances. The farmers have learned through bitter experience that they are not going to be able to borrow themselves out of trouble. The minister also pointed out that the volume of loans was less than $4 million. What a trickle that is when one considers the tremendous amount of money that has gone into production of wheat that is still on the farms and in country elevators in western Canada. The hon. member for Kindersley pointed out that the program to date has not cost the government of Canada a 5-cent piece and has not cost the banks anything. At the end of September, 1956, the amount outstanding was $140,000.
I admit that the minister has us at a bit of a disadvantage today, in that the leaders of the farm organizations apparently have come down on the minister's side. The minister said yesterday, as found at page 2161 of Hansard:
May I say, Mr. Chairman, that I have seldom brought before the house a bill which is unanimously recommended by every farm organization, but I think I can say this about the bill referred to in this motion. The three wheat pools, the Canadian federation of agriculture, the United Farmers and a great number of local organizations have asked that this bill be passed and have asked in the exact terms in which the bill has been drafted. I therefore think that hon. members will find it very simple indeed to accept this motion of the government without extended and involved debate.
My colleague the hon. member for Hum-boldt-Melfort pointed out that we are not

the servants of the wheat pool, the federation of agriculture or any of these other organizations, but are the elected representatives of the people in our various constituencies. I admit very frankly that on occasions we have found it most useful to use the opinions of these farm organizations in support of our claims, but the fact that apparently they are not concerned about this problem is not going to result in our failing to do our duty.
I have read with a good deal of care the submission of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture to the members of the cabinet on February 15 of this year. I have read and reread the section on grain and grain marketing, and I confess frankly that it is very difficult for me to understand why a farm organization would take the time to send representatives to the capital of Canada to discuss this most important matter without putting forward some of the fundamental problems and making some suggestions.
They are for the wheat board. Who is against the wheat board? Surely they did not need to come to Ottawa to say they were for the wheat board. They would like the board to be the sole marketing agency for grain in western Canada, including flax and rye. A great many people are in favour of that, but the government is not prepared to act in any great hurry.
The farmers want to do away with speculative futures for oats and barley. They would like the price for 1957-58 to be not less than the price last year. They would like to have extended storage facilities. They would like to have the bushel system discarded and to have it replaced by the hundredweight system. They would like to do something about eastern grain standards. But in the same brief they devote about as much space to the question of income tax and succession duties. I submit that no farm organization can have it both ways. They cannot argue that their industry is in a jam and then make representations that would cost the treasury so much money.
Their first proposal is to exempt estates up to $50,000. My information is that this first proposal would cost the treasury of Canada between $8 million and $10 million. Then they would like to have another $25,000 made available to the surviving spouse, which would cost another $2,500,000. In view of the fact that no farm organization that I know of in my constituency has ever become excited about the people in this category, I wonder why a farm delegation devotes so much time to getting this sort of burden placed on the taxpayers.
I have done a calculation on the position of a widow whose husband left an estate of

$100,000. It would appear that if she were the sole survivor there would be $11,760 paid as succession duties under prevailing rates. The federation of agriculture would like to have this changed so her tax would be reduced to either $2,500 or $3,700. It was not too clear exactly what they meant. But in either case I do not think there are many farmers in the prairie provinces who are excited about a poor widow who is left $100,000 who is going to have to pay $11,720 in succession duties to the treasury of Canada, or whether we should give her relief and reduce this amount to $2,500 or $3,700.
So, Mr. Chairman, in spite of the representations made by the federation of agriculture,
I maintain that the wheat farmers of Canada are facing the most serious crisis in Canadian history. We have had some discussions from time to time about the position of the farmers in the thirties. With the exception of 1932 and 1933 the farmers' share of the national income now is smaller than the farmers' share was between 1930 and 1940. The people of Canada cannot afford to see this important Canadian industry pushed to the wall and forced into bankruptcy, which will be the inevitable consequence if something is not done.
I think we should not be talking in terms of reducing production and abandoning markets. I wish the Minister of Trade and Commerce, in dealing with this responsibility of his, would exercise the same imagination he uses in connection with his responsibility as the minister in charge of T.C.A. I have read with interest the annual report that he made available yesterday. He has authorized the purchase of some 20 Vickers Vanguards, I believe, at a cost of over $5 million a plane. I read that these planes will carry 120 passengers. They will fly from Montreal to the United Kingdom and back every day if necessary. They will fly from Toronto to Vancouver and back twice every day. It is hard to figure out how we can spend $5 million for one plane and yet, according to the minister's evidence loan less than $4 million this year. All he could do to help the farmers meet the competition in their wheat marketing at the present time was to guarantee to the banks that they will not lose anything on loans.
The Minister of Agriculture is responsible for an interesting publication entitled Agriculture Abroad. I am glad the Minister of Agriculture is here in the chamber as well as the Minister of Trade and Commerce. This February number contains interesting comments on agriculture in Argentina, Australia, Belgium, Czechoslovakia, Denmark, Italy, the United Kingdom and the United States. I will not have time to refer to the reports on
Grain
all these countries, but I want to point out that each one is using substantial amounts of public funds to bolster their agriculture economy. Yet our Canadian farmers are being given only the assistance which this legislation proposes, nothing from the federal treasury, but an opportunity to continue borrowing from the chartered banks for about 15,000 people, far less than 10 per cent of all the farmers. The average loan in the first period was $764.45; the average loan in the second period was $694.87. That is a mere drop in the bucket in contrast with the cost of production.
The first section in this publication Agriculture Abroad deals with Argentina. As a part of their program to assist their farmers they are increasing the storage capacity for wheat by about 202 million tons. If the government of Canada were prepared to embark on a program of terminal elevator construction instead of putting so much of our total resources into industrial expansion, it would be possible for more of our farmers to be able to market their grain.
In Austrialia they have been able to sign a new wheat agreement with the United Kingdom, and they have set up a fund under the commonwealth stabilization act. The cost of production in Australia is a factor, and they are introducing a two-price system, one price for local consumption and one price for the wheat that is to go into the world market.
As to Belgium, it is pointed out in Agriculture Abroad:
The farmers point out that when industrial firms are forced, through increased costs, to raise the selling price of their products, there is no outcry in the press, as this is found to be normal business procedure. However, when farmers find themselves in a similar situation and propose increasing their prices to compensate, they find almost the entire press, and public opinion in general, opposed to them.
Belgium has had a program to see that the farmers who remain on the farm get a larger share of the consumer dollar.
With regard to Italy we find this:
The system under which part of the wheat crop is compulsorily collected continued during the year. The price of the wheat to be handed over is fixed by the state in relation to production costs. This tends to ensure a fair profit for the farmers, and at the same time has a regularizing effect on the market for processed products such as pasta and semolina ...	.
Effective next year, the government has decided to reduce the amount of wheat for compulsory delivery to the state collecting pools . . .
In an effort to encourage farmers to store wheat on home farms, the government also decided to increase by 50 lire a quintal (2.1 cents per bushel) per month the price to be paid farmers for that portion of their wheat subject to compulsory pooling .	.	. Prior to the above-mentioned increase, the prices paid ranged from $3.25 to $3.55 per bushel for Durum and from $2.95 to $3.15 for soft wheat.

Grain
If the government of Italy is putting into the pockets of the Italian farmer 2 cents per bushel per month for every bushel the farmer stores, and pays him an initial price ranging from $3.25 to $3.55 regardless of the world price of wheat, what a hopeless position our farmers find themselves in when this government refuses to spend a 5 cent piece to get money into the pockets of the farmers to enable them to meet their operating costs. The only course open to the farmers now is to go to the banks and pay a rate of interest that is a good deal higher than they paid before.
In the United Kingdom I find that the guaranteed price for any given commodity each year will not be less than 96 per cent of the price in the previous year. May I draw these figures to the attention of the committee. The value of the guarantees and production grants is at present $3,082 million and is to be maintained at not less than 97 i per cent of the total value of guarantees for the preceding year. Provision will be made for special price review in the event of sudden cost changes. In order to improve efficiency, they are voting another $134 million. How can Canadian farmers compete in the United Kingdom markets when the United Kingdom is using public funds to the extent of $3,082 million in price supports for the year.
Coming to the United States, where we have our real competition, we find that following four years of decline, net farm income rose in 1956 by some 4 per cent to reach $11.7 billion. Here is what is happening. As a result of having public funds available and government aids for export, agricultural exports during 1956 are estimated to have exceeded $4.1 billion, an increase of some $600 million or 30 per cent over the previous year. In the latter part of the year the export programs of the government were accelerated and accounted for a major share of the export activities.
Of the $4 billion worth of agricultural products exported, more than $1.6 billion or 40 per cent were exported under government disposal programs. The best customers for United States farm exports were Japan, United Kingdom, Canada, West Germany and the Netherlands. Canada placed third in the list of importers of United States products. Our Canadian farmers are meeting competition from the United States treasury on 40 per cent of their total exports and our Minister of Trade and Commerce, who is responsible for the operations of the wheat board, has the nerve to come to parliament in 1957 and offer this proposal as the very best that the treasury of Canada can do for this important industry.

Under public bill No. 480, in 1956 United States exports exceeded 4.5 million metric tons valued at over $550 million. Under the title P. L. 480, emergency and famine relief fund, agricultural commodities to the value of $98 million were exported, and close to $400 million has been expended for the procurement of agricultural exports under section 402 of the mutual security act.
Then this document says that during the year negotiations were concluded with India for the largest transaction ever undertaken under the title of P. L. 480. India is one of our former customers and a member of the commonwealth, but has just concluded with the United States the largest transaction in history, including a very large quantity of wheat. It is going to require 400 ships to move these commodities which are to be delivered over a period of three years. The second largest transaction was with Brazil. This agreement provides for the sale of $138.7 million, including certain ocean transportation costs, worth of agricultural commodities, of which $111 million will be wheat and flour.
On January 5 of this year the United States department of commerce announced that consideration would be given to applications for licences to export surplus agricultural commodities to Poland for United States dollars at world market prices. This change of policy applies, at the moment, only to sales for dollars. The policy regarding credit sales, barter, sales under P. L. 480, and donations to Poland by the commodity credit corporation is unchanged.
Another interesting part of their program to help the dairy farmer and agriculture in general has been in connection with the school lunch program. During the current fiscal year the United States made $100 million available for this program. They do require that state and local governments provide $4 for every dollar provided by the federal government for the purchase of farm and food products under this program. During 1956 purchases under the program included hamburger, lard, pork, eggs and turkeys, none of which is under price support. The government expended about $48 million to bolster prices of these products.
So, Mr. Chairman, a very discouraging picture is presented to the Canadian farmer. He is obliged to buy in the highest priced market in the world and he is forced to sell his products in competition with other countries every one of which is subsidizing in some way or other the production of food products.
I think the Minister of Trade and Commerce has a responsibility to come out to the prairie provinces before the summer is over and go

into the constituencies of some of the Liberal members who, incidentally have not had a word to say since this debate opened yesterday. I am sure the minister will find it difficult to convince the western farmer that he is so prosperous he is able to have a new car, a year's crop in the granary, all his debts paid and not a thing to worry about. I am sure the Minister of Agriculture will certainly not come up into the Mackenzie constituency and suggest that the farmers have been forced to sell their aeroplanes in order to get a little cash.
The position of the grain farmer is very critical. The fact that in my constituency during the last five years we have lost nearly 5,000 people, about 10 per cent of our population, when the over-all population in Canada has been increasing by nearly 15 per cent, shows that there is nothing wrong with the country except that the farmer cannot possibly continue to buy where prices are so high and sell at such low prices.
When I was home recently I called on one of the larger farm operators. A year ago the Minister of Trade and Commerce suggested that some of the men on smaller farms might have been having a little trouble but that the men on larger farms were in a very comfortable position. Well, I called on a man on one of the largest farms, consisting of two Sections of very good land. This man has established a reputation as a registered seed grower. He has sold a great deal of registered grass seed. He has a large dairy herd, but he just finds it impossible to get men who will work on the farm for the current wages. His eldest son is working in the Saskatchewan oil fields, while the second and third boys are going to school. They start milking at 5.30 every morning and they milk 13 cows. The milk is taken to town some seven miles away, on their way to school and then the boys repeat the same performance after school.
One of the boys is in his last year at high school. When his brother was home at Christmas time and told about the fabulous wages he makes in the oil fields, he said, "What is the use of continuing in high school; what is the use of staying on the farm?" There certainly must be something wrong when these two fine young Canadian boys decide not to stay on one of the finest farms in northern Saskatchewan where, if the farmer was getting anything like a decent break, they could look forward to a very interesting life.
Instead of bringing in legislation of this sort the minister should indicate that Canada wants to stay in the business of producing food for the hungry people of the world. I think it is a great reflection on our modern 82715-139
Grain
society when, in a crisis like this, with half the people of the world going hungry, Canada is unwilling to lend support to the establishment of a world food bank.
I was interested in reading the minutes of the meeting of the economic and social council of the United Nations held in Geneva on July 11 and 12 last. The food and agriculture organization made representations to the United Nations to again carry on a study with a view to establishing a world food bank. I find that the Chinese delegate pointed out that 2,000 years ago China had embarked on a program with a view to building up reserves to prevent food prices from falling too low when harvests were good, and keeping them down in times of scarcity. This delegate seemed to be all for it, and the delegates from the Netherlands, from Pakistan and from Yugoslavia all spoke in the same vein regarding the world situation. Sixty-two per cent of the world's food was being produced by the industrial countries, but though there are surpluses in some parts of the world, in the underdeveloped countries, where consumption represented 21 per cent of total consumption before the war, they had been forced to reduce their percentage to 19 per cent. But, Mr. Chairman, I was disturbed to find that the Canadian delegate, the parliamentary assistant to the Secretary of State for External Affairs, stressed the obstacles in the way. There are real problems, but I think with such a large number of competent farmers available, with so much good land in the country, we should be willing to undertake some difficult assignments.
Rather than come to parliament in the year 1957 with legislation that offers so little to the wheat producers of our country, I believe the minister should be giving the wheat board some encouragement by indicating that Canada will continue to produce maximum quantities of food, and wheat in particular, since this commodity can be stored very easily. The wheat which was stored at Churchill for the entire war period was available nearly 10 years later in as good condition as when it left the farm, and we have large areas in Canada-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO ACT EXTENDING APPLICATION, FIXING INTEREST AND INCREASING MAXIMUM
speechtext: Order. I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member, but it is my duty to advise him that his time has expired.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO ACT EXTENDING APPLICATION, FIXING INTEREST AND INCREASING MAXIMUM
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, yesterday my colleagues the hon. member for Battle River -Camrose and the hon. member for Acadia laid before the committee our views with respect to the legislation before us at the present time. For that reason I shall make my remarks particularly brief. While I realize, of

Grain
course, that possibly one could travel far afield under a resolution of this kind, I shall not do so.
Last year when this program of interim financing first became known to the Canadian public, more particularly to the Canadian farmers, I was not privileged to be here in the house and was thus unable to either hear the debates or participate in them. However, the circumstances which caused me to be absent, on the other hand, put me within easy earshot of the farmers who were to be most vitally affected by this legislation.
It was rather amazing to me to find how instantaneous the response was, and it was also very interesting to me to find that the general attitude was very much in opposition to the proposed legislation. In fact the feeling was so strong that within a very short period of time protest meetings were called by the farmers themselves. I was not able to attend any of those protest meetings; therefore it could not be said that I may have been responsible for stirring them up.
However, I did secure reports in regard to the meetings, and this is what I discovered. Farmers themselves felt convinced that this offered no solution whatsoever to the major problem confronting the agricultural industry. They regarded it as a temporary expedient. They used the word "palliative". They also felt strongly that it offered no hope of assisting those most in need of assistance. They felt at that time that those farmers who could not secure loans without this legislation and the government guarantee could not secure it, or would not be able to secure it, after the legislation had become effective.
Time has proven that in their attitude at that time they were right, Mr. Chairman, because throughout the past year, under the operation of this act, they have come to the very definite conclusion that it is no solution; that it is nothing but an expedient; that it will not help those who are in dire need of help and, in a sense, it is something they could have got along very well without.
Only very recently I had another opportunity of discussing with certain farmers in my own area the present attitude with respect to the whole situation, and their attitude with respect to the proposal now before us. In the first place they said to me, "If we could not secure the $1,500, or any part of it, what good will $3,000 be to us? It will be worthless." Then, of course, they emphasized the fact that about the easiest thing anyone could do is to go into debt, and that is not what they wanted to do, particularly when they had the asset on their own farms which, If they could sell it, would result in there 
being no necessity for borrowing. That view is a very strong view and it was extremely prevalent.
They asked me about the proposed interest rate under this amendment to the Prairie Grain Producers Interim Financing Act of 1956. I said, "I do not know and I doubt if any other member of parliament knows except the Minister of Trade and Commerce unless he has intimated to his colleagues what the government would do". I said to those farmers, "If it was going to be less than 5 per cent the minister certainly would put it in this legislation". Psychologically that would seem natural. If it were going to remain at 5 per cent there would be no need of making reference to the interest aspect of the act. I told them that I could only conclude that it was going up; how far up, I did not know. Some might say to the maximum of 6 per cent now allowable to the banks, but when governments do things you cannot always count on their being governed by regulations which govern the activities of others and I told them I could not see anything to prevent them making it considerably higher than the 6 per cent which is allowable to other institutions today.
I said a moment ago, Mr. Chairman, a very unhappy situation prevails for a farmer who has assets which one would expect to be saleable, assets of good quality which are certainly required desperately by people in other places, to have to sit there putting up lots of money to create his own storage and then having to turn around and borrow and pay interest. The interest of course reduces the already low price which his product would normally command.
I saw an interesting sight the other day. A farmer who is not what I would call a large operator but one who is operating what I would describe as an economic unit told me he had to build 24 granaries. I would say off hand they were possibly ten feet by ten feet and possibly eight feet in height. In addition he had to build one quonset-type granary and all of this was done in order to hold the grain he has. We do not even have to guess in order to ascertain how much that farmer has had to put out in order to provide that storage. He asked, "What about next year"? He may well be confronted with the very same situation next year. He told me there were others who-to use his expression-"are rather handsomely rewarded for storing grain while here I must sit storing my own and possibly having to expand those storage facilities without being paid for it and at the same time I am being offered the possible

opportunity of going to borrow a loan which is guaranteed by the government and upon which I shall definitely have to pay 5 per cent and conceivably more than 5 per cent under the new amendments."
Farmers in my own constituency within the last ten days said to me, "Our whole problem is tied in with a lack of policy and our failure to market which results directly from the lack of an effective policy". We all know of course that loans are no substitute for sales and therefore when farmers spoke about this a year ago as being an expedient or a palliative, as nothing which could rightly or properly be described as a solution to the problem, they were correct.
We in this group have stressed in the past the need for cash advances on farm stored grain where it is approved storage and we still stress this need. My personal feeling is this-of course I must relay this view to others, and acting under its prerogative the government will probably soon put me in the position where I will have to relay it to a great many people-that I have not yet heard what I would consider a sound argument in opposition to cash advances on farm stored grain. It is true that arguments have been advanced in opposition to cash advances arid those who advanced them believe they are sound arguments, but their thinking so does not necessarily make them sound.
There has been very limited use of this act. I believe the minister indicated yesterday some $8 million had been loaned in the 195556 crop year and up to January 31, 1957 approximately $4 million had been loaned. Of course I realize that could increase as borrowings take place by farmers who are confronted with the regular necessity of seeding their crops in the spring.
First of all I say there has been limited use of this act and I am going to give one or two reasons for it. The first is the extreme difficulty that exists in securing loans. You run into situations where for some good reason or another a farmer has incurred a debt. This is usually not a large debt and I would say it is a relatively small one when you consider the size of his operation. The entire debt has not been paid and in many instances the farmer is told that he simply must repay what he owes and then some consideration-and not necessarily favourable consideration-will be given to his application under the act.
We also know that in many cases loans are definitely refused not because the farmer who desires to borrow is a poor risk but because he does not happen to do business normally with a particular institution. I think 82715-139J
Grain
my colleague the hon. member for Battle River-Camrose referred to this situation yesterday. In the majority of our communities in my own province of Alberta we have branches of the provincial treasury department. Outside of acting as federal government agents the treasury branches do practically all the business chartered banks do and they do something else, too, in that they provide competition where the banks have almost eliminated competition against themselves.
We all remember the old set-up when two chartered banks already located in one community would put their heads together and one would agree to pull out of that community if the other would pull out of the next community. This situation was not peculiar to our province and it resulted in there being absolutely no competition for the bank in a community. For this as well as for many other reasons competition through treasury branches was eventually established.
I believe that most people who have a belief in democracy also believe in the private enterprise system and accept the fact that competition is a good thing. If we believe in democracy we also believe that there should be a substantial element of choice for the individual in the doing of his business. Well, of course, many of these farmers have exercised their democratic right to deal with their treasury branches.
I say that those branches, outside of activities as agents of the federal government will render all the services required. These farmers are forced to go to the branch of a chartered bank and in a great many instances they are asked where they do their business and when they reply that they do it at the treasury branch the answer often is, "You had better go down there to borrow your money". I do not say that all bank managers act that way, but it is certainly a common occurrence in some communities.
In other words, because a local citizen exercises his democratic right, as one should do in a democracy, he is being deprived of the benefits of legislation of this parliament of Canada. If you like to put it that way, there are being created various classes of citizenry, even among our farmers. This is the first time I have taken advantage of the opportunity to say this but I am wondering why it is the government could not give favourable consideration to permitting these treasury branches to serve as agents in this respect. There may be technical reasons for acting as they do, but if it were done I am sure it would eliminate a great deal of the criticism which has been directed toward the government and the Department of Trade

Grain
and Commerce by these people who are treated in this way under legislation of this kind. It is not limited just to this particular piece of legislation; we find it under other federal legislation covering government guarantees such as the Farm Improvement Loans Act.
Yesterday someone indicated that we were trying to establish in Canada a stable agricultural industry. I think our goal should be the attainment of a policy which would bring about a condition of stability. Yet most of what we are doing is of a temporary nature and involves, as a speaker said yesterday, borrowing and debt. Reference was made to the Farm Improvement Loans Act, to this act and to others. It annoys a person when in the light of successful operations on his part in connection with an industry which is considered as important to the economy as the agricultural industry he should be put in a position where whenever he turns his head to try to get a breath of air he finds himself in the process of going into debt.
As we said yesterday, as we have said time and time again and as others have said, far more serious consideration should be given to this matter of advances against farm stored grain. That is the way the farmers feel and in fact I find that merchants are thinking just as keenly of these things as are the farmers. In an area such as the one I represent, as things go for the farmer so do things go for practically everybody in the community. It is not just a matter of somebody becoming concerned about some of these things and expressing his views, we hear the merchants expressing their views quite strongly as well.
We feel of course, and we have always said, that not only should there be provision for advances against farm stored grain provided the storage is proper-I would not ask for it under any other circumstances-we are thoroughly convinced that it would be in the best interests of this nation if immediate consideration were given to the provision of greater storage space. We read every day about the vulnerability of all nations to attacks of various types. I have often thought, and I thought so even during the last war, although thank heavens this nation remained free from attack, that it was most dangerous to have these non-perishable foods and things that might spell the difference between victory and defeat concentrated at the west coast, at the head of the lakes and at Churchill.
We should have a decentralization of storage facilities, and far more in the way of storage facilities. I have heard the hon. member for Peace River urging the necessity for the provision of inland storage in the

great north country. I feel personally concerned about the fact that so much of what we have could be quickly destroyed if the worst, as far as the international situation is concerned, came to pass. I am hopeful, as are all hon. members, that such things will never occur, but it is better to be prepared than to be sorry.
I am not going to take up more time of the committee. This legislation does not meet with the approval of the farmers in my area. In fact, I find they are resentful, they do not like the idea of being forced into debt in order to secure assistance. They would prefer to see the government adopt a long-range policy so that they could hope for some stability. We find the word "interim" in the title of the act which is to be amended, and that word suggests that it is temporary.
There has just been too much done of a temporary character in relation to agriculture. If Canada is to be strong, if this industry is to be made stable, we had better be thinking in terms of something other than the Prairie Grain Producers Interim Financing Act, 1956.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO ACT EXTENDING APPLICATION, FIXING INTEREST AND INCREASING MAXIMUM
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, there seems to be a misconception about what we are trying to do. It has been assumed that the bill to follow this resolution will change the complexion of western agriculture from being in the distressed state in which we are told it is now, to a state of great prosperity. This bill proposes nothing of the kind. We were asked to enact this legislation by every farm organization in western Canada. I had thought as a matter of fact that our grain legislation could very well be deferred until the autumn, when any steps we might take could be taken in the light of the coming season's crop results.
The Canadian Federation of Agriculture, western section, met in Winnipeg about two months ago to discuss what it wanted the government to do and out of that meeting came just one request, that we increase the amount of bank accommodation under the act which is in force at the present time. I indicated at that time the government had no objection to meeting that request.
There was a second meeting attended by representatives of every farm organization in Canada which was held in Saskatoon. The three wheat pools were represented, the federation of agriculture, the farmers' union and the United Grain Growers. From this meeting came just one request. These organizations wanted larger bank loans made available, $3,000 instead of $1,500, and they wanted the effective date of the loan put back to September 1 rather than October 1 as in the present legislation. At the time

we received that message there was a resolution on the order paper and it was necessary to withdraw it and replace it with the resolution we are discussing now.
Why did we not get other requests from these meetings? I am sure both meetings discussed cash advances. That is what both meetings were held for. We received no request for cash advances. Why? Because there was no agreement as to how such a plan could be administered. I am told there was the widest difference among various groups as to what they wanted by way of machinery for cash advances. I am not suggesting that if these meetings had brought forward a plan for cash advances the government would have accepted it holus-bolus but at least we would have looked at it very carefully. The point I am making is that the organizations themselves cannot agree.
Opposition members of parliament are very much wiser. A member of the opposition can get up here and say glibly that he has a plan for cash advances. One member said, "Let the wheat board handle the advances". Somebody else said, "Let the elevator agents do it", and somebody else has another plan. What is the government going to do? Is the government going to say that it will take all these plans and put them into effect at once? Be that as it may, this resolution just deals with one matter, and that is the matter of the unanimous request from every prairie farm organization.
We have had speakers say that these organizations do not represent the farmers. I suppose every farmer is a member of some organization that was represented at the gathering at Saskatoon, and I would assume that the organizations are supposed to represent their members. If not, I am sure the heads of the organizations will be changed whenever the next meeting is held. What do I now find? I come forward with a bill in the exact form in which I was asked to have it passed. We have had three speakers from the Conservative party say that they are opposed to the bill. We have had three speakers from the Social Credit party say that they are opposed to the bill. We have had four or five speakers from the C.C.F. party say that they are opposed to the bill.
I do not know how far I need to press this legislation. I am trying to be helpful, but I think I may have to accept the inevitable. At eight o'clock tonight we have the budget. Tomorrow we have a debate on external affairs. Then we have eight more days of budget debate, and then there will be on the order paper an accumulation of bills that will have to be passed. All I need to do to clear myself is to say that
Grain
not only could I not get this bill passed but I could not even get the bill before the house. All I need to say is: "Here are two Hansards; read them and see who prevented me from placing the bill before the house." I can do that and if necessary I must do it. Of course, that is what I will do, but first I should like to let everyone understand what I am trying to do at this time.
I am not trying to solve the farm problem with this one bill. Of course I am not. I am trying to carry out the wishes of the farm organizations as they have been presented to me in resolutions from the meetings and by the delegates from the farm organizations who have been here. That is the position, and I do not know that I want to say much more about it. If we can get the bill before the house today, I will do my best to get it passed at this session, but if we cannot pass the resolution, what is the use? For two days I have been told that no one wants this bill. I will admit at once that I cannot get the bill through if it is fought for the time it was fought last year. At that time it took two and a half solid weeks to get the present act passed. We have not got two and a half solid weeks in this session to devote to this bill. That is the situation. Now, deal with it as you like.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to speak at length but I have a number of questions I should like to put to the minister. However, if the hon. member for Moose Mountain wishes to speak I think I should defer to him.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, first of all I cannot say that I share the enthusiasm of the minister about the legislation as expressed in his remarks in introducing the resolution yesterday or in the words he has uttered today which would lead the house to believe that the farm organizations are asking for this type of legislation. If the minister wants the co-operation of members of the C.C.F. group, all he needs to do is to bring into the house the legislation which the farm organizations have been asking for over the years and which they are still requesting.
This year we have had a whole crop of bills brought into the house which in my opinion are simply designed to extend more credit to the common people so that it will be a shot in the arm of a decadent system. I am convinced that the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Agriculture have, either deliberately or otherwise, disrupted, confused and perhaps coerced the leaders of the farm organizations throughout

Grain
the country in order to try to prevent them from asking for legislation to provide cash advances.
