speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I have just had an aspersion cast on my character by my hon. friend. He says that I have coerced the leaders of the farm organization in an attempt to avoid bringing legislation before the house. I deny it absolutely, and I ask my hon. friend to withdraw his statement.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO ACT EXTENDING APPLICATION, FIXING INTEREST AND INCREASING MAXIMUM
speechtext: It is not unparliamentary.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO ACT EXTENDING APPLICATION, FIXING INTEREST AND INCREASING MAXIMUM
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I am quite prepared to take the minister's statement and withdraw. I am simply saying that when the Canadian Federation of Agriculture had Mr. Benson come to Regina two years ago and he indicated to the federation that the system employed in the United States under the Commodity Credit Corporation was a failure and the government of that country was backing away from the program of giving cash advances to farmers, that in itself was the first step in trying to coerce the membership of farm organizations to move away from the demand for cash advances on grain properly stored on farms.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO ACT EXTENDING APPLICATION, FIXING INTEREST AND INCREASING MAXIMUM
speechtext: May I ask my hon. friend if he is suggesting that Mr. Benson was a party to his suggested plot to coerce the farmers of Canada?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO ACT EXTENDING APPLICATION, FIXING INTEREST AND INCREASING MAXIMUM
speechtext:
I am
convinced that there has been a plot on the part of certain people in Canada at least to undermine the concerted effort that has been made to obtain cash advances, and I am going to put on the record the demands of the farm organizations for cash advances on farm-stored grain. In his speech yesterday the minister said, as found at page 2161 of Hansard:
May I say, Mr. Chairman, that I have seldom brought before the house a bill which is unanimously recommended by every farm organization, but I think I can say this about the bill referred to in this motion.
I want to put on record what the farm organizations have been requesting. I have here the resolutions passed at the annual meeting of wheat pool delegates in 1955 and I am going to read some of them into the record because I think they are important. In part they have this to say:
2.	That we urge the government of Canada to make immediate provision for advances to farmers on farm stored grain.
3.	That advances to farmers on farm stored grain should be up to one-half the normal delivery expected and repayable on the basis of one-half of the value of each delivery made by the farmer.
4.	That advances on farm stored grain should be made by way of government guaranteed loans

to the Canadian wheat board; the Canadian wheat board to arrange with elevator companies to make the advances to individual farmers; and further,
That any interest involved in such loans should be absorbed by the federal treasury.
I think that is a far cry from what we have before the house today. They say further:
5.	Whereas deliveries of grain to elevators may be curtailed over fairly long cycles, due to congested handling facilities, and since these curtailments in deliveries will create a frequent need for short term credit;
Be it resolved that the board of directors give consideration to drafting a plan that will permanently meet the need for advances on farm stored grain, and that this plan be presented to the next annual meeting of delegates.
I now want to quote from a letter of the Saskatchewan Farmers Union of March 12, 1957 with respect to that Saskatchewan Farmers Union attitude towards cash advances. In this letter it is stated as follows:
The official policy of the Saskatchewan Farmers Union with respect to cash advances on farm stored grain remains as it has always been-that is for cash advances through the elevator companies advanced on the basis of half the expected delivery quota, interest free, to the Canadian wheat board.
I think that again contradicts the statement of the minister that the farm organizations are in any way whipped into accepting this iniquitous resolution now before us which is going to make the farmer practically get down on his knees before the chartered banks in order to get an advance on his farm stored grain.
I want to quote further from a letter of March 5, 1957 under the signature of Rudolph Usick who is an official of the farmers union of Manitoba:
Since the Prairie Grain Producers Interim Financing Act is up for amendment in the House of Commons I thought I should mention a meeting of ten organizations held in Saskatoon on Friday, March 1.
I might interject here, Mr. Chairman, in order to say that this reference is to the meeting to which the minister just referred before he left his seat. I continue the quotation from the letter:
At this meeting a resolution was passed and sent by telegram to Messrs. Howe, Gardiner, Harris and St. Laurent. No press release was issued because they wanted the government to have an opportunity to study the proposal.
This resolution was as follows, and I quote the telegram:
Resolved that while we do not agree that the Prairie Grain Producers Interim Financing Act is the most satisfactory method for making money available on grain that cannot be delivered however in view of the late date in having a more satisfactory plan for cash advances adopted at this session of parliament this committee recommends-
In connection with that, Mr. Chairman, I want to point out again that this resolution before us does not meet fully what is asked

for in this request because paragraph (d) of the request says this:
(d) that interest rates be as low as possible and in any event not higher than that paid by Canadian wheat board.
Under the resolution before us we have no guarantee of what the interest rate will be. I presume that the interest rate will be the prevailing interest rate which it is necessary to charge and it might very well be higher than 5 per cent.
I think that this fairly well proves conclusively that the farm organizations are accepting this as a third rate compromise. They are not accepting it as something that they want. They consider it to be unfair. Every single farmer in western Canada does not consider this justice by any means. I feel that it is in effect a brazen disregard of farm organization demands over the years. I should like to hear what the Saskatchewan backbenchers have to say with regard to this matter. When they go back to their constituents, Mr. Chairman, I am sure they are not going to be able to support this iniquitous legislation we have before this house. If we are obliged to accept it, then it is going to be as a deathbed acceptance. I want to say to the Minister of Trade and Commerce that if he wants the co-operation of this group- and I can speak only for the C.C.F. group-all he needs to bring in is some kind of legislation more in line with the demands of farm organizations in western Canada, and I am sure we will expedite that legislation passage through the house.
We have further, Mr. Chairman, the situation of the three western Canadian wheat pools which on March 9 of this year-just Saturday of last week-in a brief or submission presented to the federal cabinet said they wanted a reduction in the interest rate on grain loans. Again this legislation does not even meet this demand or submission to the federal government as of March 9 of this year.
The farmers in western Canada are in a cost-price squeeze. This legislation is going to mean that even those who get loans are going to have to go out and in effect borrow on their year's earnings and pay at least 5 per cent interest on their wages. That is exactly what it means. I do not think there can be an hon. member in this house who will support that proposal as being fair. So, as we have said time and time again, we support the idea of cash advances on farm stored grain, properly stored under a plan similar to that which they have had in the United States for some 17 years or more. I was down in the United States two years ago. I went there for the express purpose of finding out if this drive in the United States
Grain
to try to discredit the United States program under the commodity credit corporation had any justification. I think hon. members will know that there was in the United States a drive by the United States government to move away from the plan under the commodity credit corporation. Mr. Benson, the minister of agriculture in the United States, was sent out to all the agricultural states in order to try to get the farmers to agree to a loan price formula or support formula for farm stored grain. At that time it was 90 per cent of parity. The intent was to try to bring in some type of flexible parity for farm stored grain. It is interesting to note that since two years ago the United States government has moved back to a greater rigidity in price support and closer to the 90 per cent of parity. But as I say, in this country there is no regard paid to the farmer's costs and the farmer finds himself in a cost-price squeeze. I do not share the minister's fears that this would in any way jeopardize the Canadian wheat board. I think it is in effect holding the big stick over the farm organizations when the minister gets to his feet in this house and says that if we had the Canadian wheat board implement ing a plan through which payment could be made to farmers on farm stored grain, it would jeopardize the Canadian wheat board. I think it is sheer nonsense because we have today in western Canada the plan whereby the farmers must, in order to sell their grain, deliver to the elevator under quota. At the elevator they have their quota books and each delivery is recorded in their quota books. Under the present plan, when that wheat is delivered, the farmer gets a payment on his delivered grain. Subsequently, he gets interim payments until the final payment is made. Under the plan which could be involved under payments on farm stored grain, the farmer would get an advance after the assurance was made by the elevator agent, municipal officials or somebody else, as to grain in store and he would be paid in advance on his farm stored grain. If this government was prepared to set up a treasury fund at the disposal of the Canadian wheat board, similar to the present system of payment for grain delivered, in order to pay for cash advances so that the Canadian wheat board could pay on farm stored grain, there would be no difficulty whatever in putting it into effect. The full responsibility lies on the treasury benches of this government. So I say that if any farm organization has agreed to accept this legislation, they have done so not because they agree with it but because the western farmers-some of them at least- are in dire straits and are needing cash.

Grain
At this time, Mr. Chairman, the situation is that about one-third of the western marketing points are still on a two-bushel quota. How can a western farmer pay his fuel bills, his grocery bills and carry on in the face of a situation of that kind? In my constituency I have seen farmers selling cattle which should have been on feed and sold at a later time. These cattle have been sold simply because the farmer was forced to get some ready cash.
The hon. member who preceded me indicated that this is not only the problem of the farmer, it is the problem of everyone living in western communities. It is a problem of local financing. It is the problem of the merchant, the fuel dealer: all these people are up against the problem of trying to carry on and the members of the Liberal party have not seen fit to get up in this house and try to get this government to give the western farmers a better deal. I can only say again that I do not see any difficulty in the way of the Canadian wheat board being designated as the means through which advances could be made. I do not believe for a moment the statement made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce that these wheat board officials would resign if they were asked to do this job. I cannot conceive of it. I feel that there is really no problem there. I think it is just a bogey man put before this parliament. Of course, the leaders of farm organizations read what the minister says in this house and they are frightened away from asking for a better plan. I hope that even at this late date the minister will see fit to withdraw this resolution and bring in a resolution prefacing a bill which will meet the needs of western Canadian farmers.
I might point out that so far there have been no losses in connection with the operation of this program. There is approximately $140,000 outstanding, but I believe that is all receivable. If we have the sort of a program under which a farmer has to have wheat on his farm to the value of twice the amount of the loan he is requesting, then I think the government or the Canadian wheat board would be very safe indeed. I want to say further that any recommendations which farm organizations have made to this government have been made in addition to, and along with, other recommendations. Some of the recommendations go so far as to ask for better promotional deals in connection with the sale of wheat.
This government has put the responsibility for the sale of wheat on the Canadian wheat board. In other words, it says that the Canadian wheat board is responsible for the kind

of deals which we make with foreign countries. The program of this government so far has been cash on the barrel head. We in this group have advocated-I might say, Mr. Chairman, it is in conformity with resolutions which I could read into the record from the farm union, the wheat pools and the Canadian federation of agriculture-that this government should wake up and try to get some barter deals or some deals whereby we take local currency in line with the program developed in the United States under the commodity credit corporation. It is sheer nonsense for this government to think that trade is a one-way street. If we are not going to take imports from other countries but we expect them to buy our grain, then of course that situation cannot continue very long.
I was annoyed last fall, and I think a lot of western farmers were annoyed, when it was announced that the government criticized Washington because the United States had undertaken an agreement with Brazil for the sale of 1,800 tons of wheat over a three or four year period in return for goods from Brazil. Instead of protesting, I think this government should wake up and try to get some plan whereby we can sell Canadian wheat. It is quite evident that this can be done. No amount of protest is going to change conditions so that we can compete with other countries which are prepared to undertake deals of this kind.
Just about two weeks ago it was announced here that the Canadian farmer would be asked to aid Canadian millers in competing with the United States treasury. Today the western farmer is in a cost-price squeeze. He cannot accept the extra burden of trying to compete with United States millers. We have heard how the price of export flour would be lowered by 4.5 cents to eight cents and that is going to be paid by the western farmer. I think, Mr. Chairman, the time has come for a day of reckoning. It is true, as the hon. member for Mackenzie has indicated, that a number of farmers are leaving the farms to go into other occupations. I happen to live in one of the most favoured constituencies in western Canada, a very fine mixed farming community. However, I can quite honestly tell this house that just before I came down to this session I was talking with what I thought was one of the more prosperous farmers. This man farms on a big scale and has 15 or 16 quarter sections of land. He raises 200 or 300 head of cattle.
This farmer told me that his two sons have decided to take up farming but he wondered whether or not it would be advisable for them to do so. Here is a man who is coming to the conclusion that we cannot continue in this

cost-price squeeze in western Canada. Here is one of our better farmers wondering whether or not his own sons should stay on the farm. Now, we have this government once more placing the burden on the western farmer through this legislation.
I had hoped in all seriousness, Mr. Chairman, that this government might still see fit to agree to some of the things we in this group have advocated. I hope the minister will see fit to withdraw this resolution and bring in a resolution which will provide for cash advances to farmers in western Canada on farm stored grain. I feel that is not asking for anything unfair. The farmer has very little say today in the marketing of his wheat. He is quite prepared to market it through the Canadian wheat board. We in this group want orderly production, we want orderly marketing and we want legislation which will protect the farmer in carrying out his duties.
In conclusion, may I say that I do not think the minister can leave the impression in this house that there is any farm organization which accepts this measure. I do not think the curfew has been rung on this session of parliament. We still will have a couple of weeks. If this government were really sincere in trying to meet the wishes of the western farmer and were prepared to introduce such legislation, every member of this group would agree to expedite it through the house.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO ACT EXTENDING APPLICATION, FIXING INTEREST AND INCREASING MAXIMUM
speechtext:
May I now put certain questions to the minister designed to elicit information which I think ought to be before the committee and has not yet been given to it. As I understand it, no report has been issued by the government as yet on the operations under this Prairie Grain Producers Financing Act which came into effect a year ago. In his opening statement yesterday, at page 2161 of Hansard, the minister gave some partial information and perhaps my questions could lead on from that point.
He said:
During the crop year 1955-56 producers borrowed a little less than $8 million. Practically all of these advances have already been repaid. Up-to-date records on the current year are not yet available from the banks, but as of January 31, 1957 the volume was less than $4 million.
Has the minister the figures for the number of loans in those two years?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO ACT EXTENDING APPLICATION, FIXING INTEREST AND INCREASING MAXIMUM
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am sorry I do not have that information. This act is administered by the Department of Finance, which is dealing with the banks. I have not an accurate report but I believe, speaking from memory and subject to correction, that the amounts borrowed in the
Grain
first year were something like $14 million. My hon. friend will realize that these grain loans have a fairly quick turnover. The amount of the borrowing is half the value of the grain that the borrower expects to deliver within that year. As he delivers that grain, the loan is repaid. The result is that on the first year's operation practically all the money has been repaid; within a few thousand dollars, I believe. This year the reports from the banks run about two months behind the month for which the reports are being made and I have no figures later than the end of January. At that time we were told the total borrowings were about $4 million. I cannot say how many borrowers were involved.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO ACT EXTENDING APPLICATION, FIXING INTEREST AND INCREASING MAXIMUM
speechtext: No doubt that information could be obtained-

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO ACT EXTENDING APPLICATION, FIXING INTEREST AND INCREASING MAXIMUM
speechtext: I would be glad to obtain it.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO ACT EXTENDING APPLICATION, FIXING INTEREST AND INCREASING MAXIMUM
speechtext: -from the Department of Finance. It may be that the same fate will confront a number of other questions I have here. If the minister has not the information, perhaps he could arrange to obtain it before we come to a later stage of the measure.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO ACT EXTENDING APPLICATION, FIXING INTEREST AND INCREASING MAXIMUM
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO ACT EXTENDING APPLICATION, FIXING INTEREST AND INCREASING MAXIMUM
speechtext:
Perhaps I might just indicate the questions that I have as requiring information which I think ought to be before the house. If the minister has the information perhaps he would give it; if not, perhaps he would undertake to obtain it before we reach the next stage of the measure.
I should like to know the number of loans in each of the two years and their distribution by provinces, if information is available on that basis. Next, the average amount of the loans; a figure was given by one hon. member yesterday that $704 was the average amount of loan. I think we should have the official figure on that.
Next, I should like to know how many loans of the maximum permissible amount were made, and then whether any claims have been made on the government on the guarantees that have been given for the loans.
On the next matter, Mr. Chairman, I think the information is within the minister's knowledge now. May I take it that the proposed increase in the permissible maximum amount of $3,000 is not intended to have any effect on the permissible maximum guarantee permitted under section 4 of the act? You will remember that there are two forms of over-all guarantee applicable to the totality of operations under the act that were written into section 4 of the act. I take it there is no intention to alter this in the bill-

Grain

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO ACT EXTENDING APPLICATION, FIXING INTEREST AND INCREASING MAXIMUM
speechtext: That is correct.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO ACT EXTENDING APPLICATION, FIXING INTEREST AND INCREASING MAXIMUM
speechtext: -because the amounts that have been guaranteed fall so far short in the past year of the $50 million maximum that there is no question, even with the proposed increase in the maximum individual loan to $3,000, of coming anywhere near the $50 million total maximum permitted.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO ACT EXTENDING APPLICATION, FIXING INTEREST AND INCREASING MAXIMUM
speechtext: That is correct, Mr. Chairman. There is no intention to enlarge the amount of the guarantee. This new maximum limit accommodates farmers who have a larger operation than those who have been taking advantage of the loan to date. A farmer must have $6,000 worth of grain deliverable in the year in order to borrow the $3,000, and there are not too many farmers who have that; that is, there is not a large proportion of the total who have that much deliverable grain.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO ACT EXTENDING APPLICATION, FIXING INTEREST AND INCREASING MAXIMUM
speechtext: The next question, Mr. Chairman, relates to the interest rate. May I take it, Mr. Chairman, that all the loans that have been made thus far under the act with respect to the two crop years 1955-56 and 1956-57 have been at the rate of 5 per cent?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO ACT EXTENDING APPLICATION, FIXING INTEREST AND INCREASING MAXIMUM
speechtext:
Yes, that is correct. Unless the loan is made at 5 per cent or under it is not guaranteed by the government. That is inherent in the legislation.
I can now answer earlier questions. I have some new information. The loans in the first year of operation were 10,326 for an amount of $7,893,830.32. In the second year, up to January 31, 1957, the number of loans totalled 5,034 for an amount of $3,498,011.67.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO ACT EXTENDING APPLICATION, FIXING INTEREST AND INCREASING MAXIMUM
speechtext: I take it the minister has not it broken down by provinces?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO ACT EXTENDING APPLICATION, FIXING INTEREST AND INCREASING MAXIMUM
speechtext: No, I have not.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO ACT EXTENDING APPLICATION, FIXING INTEREST AND INCREASING MAXIMUM
speechtext: Let me come back to this matter of the interest rate, Mr. Chairman. It will be remembered that we had some spirited discussion a year ago with regard to the clause dealing with the interest rate, and the committee, I am sure, will not need to be reminded that the maximum rate set in the bill was 5 per cent. It is quite proper to guarantee a loan at a lower rate of interest if there were any such. The minister has indicated that all the loans under the act with respect to the two crop years have been at the maximum rate of 5 per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO ACT EXTENDING APPLICATION, FIXING INTEREST AND INCREASING MAXIMUM
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am not sure of that fact. The act permitted loans to be made at a rate not higher than 5 per cent. I would not know whether there had been loans made a a lower rate than that. They would simply be reported as guaranteed loans. The matter of the interest rate is between the borrower and his bank, with 
the understanding that if the loan was not 5 per cent or lower it could not be guaranteed by the government; no recovery would be possible from the government guarantee.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO ACT EXTENDING APPLICATION, FIXING INTEREST AND INCREASING MAXIMUM
speechtext: I would ask the minister to check the figures that he gave the committee a moment ago for the second year. I think he said 5 million.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO ACT EXTENDING APPLICATION, FIXING INTEREST AND INCREASING MAXIMUM
speechtext: In the first year, there were 10,326 loans; in the second year, 5,034. If I said 5 million it was a mistake.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO ACT EXTENDING APPLICATION, FIXING INTEREST AND INCREASING MAXIMUM
speechtext: I think it is very unlikely that there were any loans made below the permissible maximum of 5 per cent, but that information should be available and could be obtained.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO ACT EXTENDING APPLICATION, FIXING INTEREST AND INCREASING MAXIMUM
speechtext: I do not know that it is possible. I do not imagine that if loans were made at a lower rate that fact would be reported. We are not interested in the rate except that it must not be higher than 5 per cent.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO ACT EXTENDING APPLICATION, FIXING INTEREST AND INCREASING MAXIMUM
speechtext:
I appreciate that. The
guarantee, under the act, cannot be given if the loan is at a rate in excess of 5 per cent, but as to whether all the loans were made at 5 per cent or less we have no information yet and I think it should be available. I think it is a pretty good guess on the part of any member of this house that no loans were ever made at a rate below 5 per cent.
Very little information has been given to the committee thus far by the minister with regard to that feature of the resolution that proposes to remove from the act the clear stipulation as to the maximum rate of 5 per cent per annum simple interest and to substitute for that a new power in favour of the governor in council to establish a maximum rate. I think the minister ought to give the committee information on this subject and indicate to us what has suggested the necessity for any departure from the present provision. Is the pressure on this interest rate upward, and where is the pressure coming from? Is there any indication that the banks are not prepared to lend at the 5 per cent so that loans made by them would not qualify for the guarantee under the act?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO ACT EXTENDING APPLICATION, FIXING INTEREST AND INCREASING MAXIMUM
speechtext: Frankly, the government feels that this is not the time to establish a maximum rate for a period that begins some months hence. I would remind my hon. friend that the rich and powerful province of Ontario paid something more than 5 per cent for its recent borrowing of, I think, $100 million.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO ACT EXTENDING APPLICATION, FIXING INTEREST AND INCREASING MAXIMUM

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO ACT EXTENDING APPLICATION, FIXING INTEREST AND INCREASING MAXIMUM
speechtext: Issued to the public at 5 per cent. The net to the province of Ontario must have been a figure that would cost the province something more than 5 per cent.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO ACT EXTENDING APPLICATION, FIXING INTEREST AND INCREASING MAXIMUM
speechtext: I saw it quoted yesterday at 4.96, I think.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO ACT EXTENDING APPLICATION, FIXING INTEREST AND INCREASING MAXIMUM
speechtext: To the province?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO ACT EXTENDING APPLICATION, FIXING INTEREST AND INCREASING MAXIMUM
speechtext: That is the going rate now; the effective rate of return.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO ACT EXTENDING APPLICATION, FIXING INTEREST AND INCREASING MAXIMUM
speechtext: You mean that is the over-all rate of return from the loan?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO ACT EXTENDING APPLICATION, FIXING INTEREST AND INCREASING MAXIMUM
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO ACT EXTENDING APPLICATION, FIXING INTEREST AND INCREASING MAXIMUM
speechtext: I do not know; I do not want to argue that point. We are not far apart but I suggest the bonds cost the province something more than 5 per cent. In other words, they would be sold at a discount below the 5 per cent return to the brokers. However, I am just pointing out that if the rich province of Ontario at this moment is paying around 5 per cent for its money it is not a good time to make a deal with the banks as to what interest they will charge the farmers beginning next September.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO ACT EXTENDING APPLICATION, FIXING INTEREST AND INCREASING MAXIMUM
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I think the minister might have come more directly to the point. We are dealing with loans that are going to have a dominion government guarantee attached to them.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO ACT EXTENDING APPLICATION, FIXING INTEREST AND INCREASING MAXIMUM
speechtext: Well, Mr. Chairman, is a dominion government guaranteed loan better than a direct obligation of the province of Ontario?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO ACT EXTENDING APPLICATION, FIXING INTEREST AND INCREASING MAXIMUM
speechtext: I do not think it is as good.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO ACT EXTENDING APPLICATION, FIXING INTEREST AND INCREASING MAXIMUM
speechtext:
We are not talking about a dominion guarantee of a provincial government obligation but we are talking about a loan to be guaranteed by the dominion government. So far the dominion government has not paid a rate like that on any of its borrowings or on any borrowings that it has guaranteed.
Now, why do we not come to the point? Is it the conclusion of the government that the interest rate of 5 per cent which is now fixed by the act as a maximum is going to have the effect of discouraging the use of this act so there will not be loans guaranteed under the provisions because the bank would not be lending at a rate as low as 5 per cent?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO ACT EXTENDING APPLICATION, FIXING INTEREST AND INCREASING MAXIMUM
speechtext:
I simply say that I do not think any man is wise enough to forecast what the interest rate situation will be in the autumn of this year and I think any man would be foolish to negotiate today for
Grain
a rate which will apply next autumn and which might be obtainable at a lower figure at that time.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO ACT EXTENDING APPLICATION, FIXING INTEREST AND INCREASING MAXIMUM
speechtext: What the minister is saying in effect is that the interest rate may be expected to go up before the autumn and that he wants to be in a position to deal with that likelihood; is that not about the way it stands?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO ACT EXTENDING APPLICATION, FIXING INTEREST AND INCREASING MAXIMUM
speechtext: I hope the interest rate will go down. If it goes up I would have been wiser to deal now. I believe interest rates are now at or near the peak. I am hoping we will get a lower interest rate by autumn. Remember this is a deal made between the government and the banks.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO ACT EXTENDING APPLICATION, FIXING INTEREST AND INCREASING MAXIMUM
speechtext:
That is surely an astonishing answer for the minister to make, Mr. Chairman, because if the effective rate the banks wish to charge is going to fall then we do not need to interfere with the provisions of the act because the act simply stipulates a maximum below which a loan may be made without any offence at all to the act, and there is no need to take unto the governor in council power to fix the interest rate if it is likely to go down. What the minister in effect is asking is the removal of the ceiling imposed by the act on the effective rate.
Whatever may be the hope that the interest rate may go down, is it not a fact that the contingency which the minister contemplates and which he gives as the reason for the removal of the statutory maximum is that he expects the interest rate is going to go up?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO ACT EXTENDING APPLICATION, FIXING INTEREST AND INCREASING MAXIMUM
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I would not attempt to deceive the farmers of western Canada. If the rate fixed under the bill is not a workable rate-in other words if the bank will not lend on that rate with a government guarantee-what good is the legislation?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO ACT EXTENDING APPLICATION, FIXING INTEREST AND INCREASING MAXIMUM
speechtext: We are getting closer to the point now, but I do wish to have this point clearly stated. The only basis the government has for asking the house to remove the maximum rate that is fixed by the statute on these loans is the contemplation of the government that the interest rate the banks are going to demand on loans to the farmers is going to rise.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO ACT EXTENDING APPLICATION, FIXING INTEREST AND INCREASING MAXIMUM
speechtext:
We face that possibility but it is by no means the only possibility. If my hon. friend is endeavouring to tell me it will go up, I say I do not know. I have considerable confidence in the powers of persuasion of the federal government and they will be used to the utmost to hold the interest rate down to the level of the present bill. But to undertake to loan money to farmers at a maximum rate of 5 per cent

Grain
when the banks may not be willing to lend money at that rate is only deceiving the farmers and I am not prepared to do that. I am prepared for any eventuality.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO ACT EXTENDING APPLICATION, FIXING INTEREST AND INCREASING MAXIMUM
speechtext: It is not a question of deceiving the farmers but rather it is a question of being frank with the house as to what may be expected and what is the real reason for asking for the removal of the statutory maximum.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO ACT EXTENDING APPLICATION, FIXING INTEREST AND INCREASING MAXIMUM
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, is this not a "having regard to" clause for the banks? The minister is quite familiar with the meaning of that term from the United Kingdom wheat agreement.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO ACT EXTENDING APPLICATION, FIXING INTEREST AND INCREASING MAXIMUM
speechtext: I do not know anything about it.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the hon. member is referring I imagine to the question he asked concerning the possibility of a new postal station being established in the vicinity of Somerled and Walkley avenues in Montreal to cover that part of the riding of Notre Dame de Grace served by the Snowden postal station. I said at the time that I would ask for a report on the matter and I can now say that from a survey made of the region by the officials they are of the opinion that it is quite probable that a new postal station will be established eventually to serve that area.
However, it is felt that when the new station is established it should not be established in the location suggested by the hon. member but rather in the Cote St. Luc area to serve the western part which is progressing and developing so rapidly at the present time. We are now considering the possibility of establishing at an early date a letter carrier depot to serve the Cote St. Luc area to which would be transferred some of the routes now served by the Snowden postal station. This matter is being looked into at the present time by the postal authorities in Montreal.
The immediate result would be to transfer thirteen routes which now originate at the Snowden postal station to the new letter

carrier depot thereby bringing the starting point of the carriers nearer to the area to be served and bringing about an earlier delivery of mail during the day.

Can
the minister tell us when that survey with regard to the location was made?

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: It was made last fall. The survey was started in December and the postmaster in Montreal did make one report which we discussed. Then on January 24 we asked for a final decision, which is what I have just told the hon. member.

The reply I received from the Postmaster General was that these plans-I am simply relying on my memory now-had been approved and that the matter was now within the jurisdiction of the Minister of Public Works.
Since the Minister of Public Works only received a copy of the letter perhaps I could not have expected a reply from him. I do not know what the convention is in that regard, but at any rate he did not reply. A week or two ago I wrote to him again and as yet I have had no reply. speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to urge upon the Postmaster General that as the minister responsible for a very large group of the civil servants who work for the federal government he might have his department make its own study of the practice of collective bargaining, particularly in the United Kingdom. I raise this question because, as the Postmaster General is aware, the matter was discussed when the Canadian Labour Congress presented its annual brief to the government of Canada on January 23, 1057. At that time the Canadian Labour Congress had in its brief an important section dealing with government employees and it made a number of requests. I shall quote one sentence from page 30:
We ask you-
This was addressed to the government, of course.
-to establish a regulated bargaining procedure for these purposes-
For the purpose of setting wages and salaries and arranging for bargaining conditions. -and to provide for the settlement of differences between the government and representative organizations of your employees through conciliation and voluntary resort to arbitration when necessary.
What was interesting about the request of the trade union movement this year for collective bargaining for the civil service was the reply of the Prime Minister. That reply was reported in the daily press at the time but I should like to read a paragraph from Canadian Labour, the official magazine of the Canadian Labour Congress, as published in February of this year. The paragraph to which I refer reads as follows:

One of the most important comments made by the Prime Minister referred to the request of the congress for recognition by the government of the right of civil servants to bargain collectively regarding wages and working conditions. Mr. St. Laurent said, "As you know, we have been of the opinion that collective bargaining could not operate within the Canadian civil service, as public servants are not employees of the government as such, but of the people of Canada." However, he was surprised to learn that a system of collective bargaining exists for the civil service in Great Britain, and he had asked to have a full study made of the method by which it operates. The information obtained would be studied most carefully by the government, with a view to determining what could be done to maintain harmonious relationships within the civil service.
I recognize the fact that the Prime Minister made the promise that this information as to the practices in Great Britain would be studied with respect to the civil service as a whole. But I make the appeal to the Postmaster General that he have his department make its own study of this matter. I would suggest that he obtain such information as he can from his own opposite number in the government of the United Kingdom. I would also draw to his attention the fact that in the United Kingdom there are some rather large unions of postal employees that have collective bargaining arrangements with the post office department of that country. For example, I find that there are over 160,000 members of the Union of Post Office Workers. It is the largest group of postal employees. There are one or two other unions as well. In case I have persuaded the Postmaster General to take up my suggestion I would tell him that the secretary of the union is Mr. C. J. Geddes, C. B. E., U. P. W. House, Crescent Lane, Clapham Common, London, S. W. 4.
I should like to suggest that the Postmaster General communicate with the postmaster general in the government of the United Kingdom and also with the secretary of the Union of Post Office Workers in order to ascertain what their practices are, in the hope that the day may not be far distant when collective bargaining will be instituted in the postal service here.
It is well known to the Postmaster General that the post office employees themselves in this country have been seeking collective bargaining for some considerable time. In view of the promise made by the Prime Minister on January 23 I would hope that the government would study the whole question in relation to the civil service and that a particular study of this matter would be made by the Postmaster General.

Mr. Chairman, last week I had occasion to point out to the Postmaster General (Mr. Lapointe) what I termed an injustice being committed in Montreal and which was to come into effect last week, that is to say last Sunday, March 10. The day after my intervention, the Montreal newspaper La Presse gave a fairly substantial account of the orders issued by the Montreal postmaster.
Convinced as I then was, and still am, that the minister was quite unaware of the decision taken, I should like to ask him this afternoon if he has instructed the Montreal postmaster to keep granting postal employees the time previously allowed them for the purpose of attending mass on Sundays, and on feast days of obligation when they are required to work.
Could the minister answer my question?

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, first of all, I must point out that holidays and time off allowed on certain occasions are determined by the civil service commission. I must also inform the house that the regulation which governs the time allowed post office employees to attend religious services, of whatever denomination, is the same as in other federal departments. That regulation provides that sufficient time be allowed those who are normally called upon to work during hours when religious services are held, so that they may attend such services. However, time thus allowed is not taken off the eight hour tour of duty. In other words, if a man normally goes off duty at four o'clock in the afternoon, and took forty-five minutes' time off in the morning to attend mass during his working hours, his working time on that day will end at 4.45 p.m.
Time off allowed a civil servant to attend religious services is not taken off his day's work; such has always been the rule prescribed by the civil service commission.
I have ascertained that this practice would be followed in the Montreal post office as it is in any other post office in this country as well as other federal government departments.
This applies particularly in the case of attendance at mass on Sunday. As regards days of obligation, the department may, at its discretion, grant the necessary time to attend religious services, and this is standard practice.

Does not the hon. minister recognize that there previously was a well

Supply-Post Office
established regulation or tradition in the Post Office Department, particularly in Montreal, tp the effect that, on the eight hour day's work of those employees, they were allowed three quarters of an hour to attend mass on Sunday?
I am referring to Sunday mass as it concerns Roman Catholic employees. However, I should not like to discriminate against anyone, and would be in favour of allowing other employees to attend religious services whatever their religious denomination.
Judging from the information published by La Presse on March 9, last I come to the conclusion that such time was taken from the eight hour day's work of postal employees.

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: I can assure the hon. member that at no time has the postmaster been authorized to grant such leave to postal employees, but he has always been free to allow them to attend religious services, provided such time be recovered in the course of the day's work. I do not know whether any tradition existed but there surely was no regulation to that effect. Consequently, if such had been the practice, it was being done without authorization. Whether it has been a tradition, I do not know, but I can assure the hon. member that this is the practice which has invariably been followed in the federal administration, in all departments, and that it is the practice followed in every other post office in this country.
If the hon. minister will allow me, I shall quote from a report of La Presse of Saturday last-

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, it is not necessary, I have read that article.

Mr. Chairman, even if the hon. minister has read that article, I feel it is important that it be read to the house, as it contradicts the statements he has just made. The article is entitled:
Sunday work for postal workers.
The employees of the central post office will have to put in their eight-hour day.
From now on employees of the Montreal Central Post Office who work on Sundays, either regularly or irregularly, will have to attend mass on their own time. The formerly allowed forty-five minute period will be discontinued starting tomorrow, March 10.
Incidentally, Mir. Chairman, may I say that if time off previously allowed has been discontinued, this is clear inference that it existed. Therefore, if there was no definite regulation to that effect, as stated by the

hon. minister, there was at least a tradition which allowed time off to employees, or which perhaps gave the postmaster discretion to grant such time off.
I am not going to read the whole article, because it is not necessary, but I would merely point out that, at the close, it states:
It is felt, at the Post Office, that employees have ample opportunity to attend the early morning masses (i.e. at 6 a.m. in several churches) or even in the late afternoon (5.15 p.m.) at Notre-Dame.
I wonder, Mr. Chairman, why they specify Notre Dame church. To attend mass at 6 a.m., a postal employee who has to work right downtown, say at the corner of Craig and Windsor, and who lives in Ahuntsic, somewhere in northern Montreal, or again in Ville St. Laurent or Ville St. Michel, would then have to get up at five o'clock. If he has to report for work at 7.45 and doesn't want to be late-because everyone knows what happens to a postal employee in Montreal when he is late-he will have to wait till he is through, at 4.30 p.m., to attend mass at 5.15 at Notre Dame church. He will then have to travel from his place of work to Notre Dame church, spend there three-quarters of an hour or one hour at the religious service and take a further hour to get home.
I believe that the explanation given by the postmaster, and that given this afternoon by the hon. minister are anything but encouraging for the postal employees. In my opinion the statement by the minister to the effect that the regulations are the same in every department, is not quite accurate. It is well known that here in Ottawa, in the province of Ontario, on days of obligation, the various departments grant their employees one hour to attend religious services. If an employee starts working at nine, he is granted the privilege to report at ten, and I do not believe the hon. minister can deny that. If there has been a regulation established by the civil service commission, it certainly has not been followed in the past. May I say again that in Montreal, until March the 10th last, i.e. up until four days ago, on the eight hour period a postal employee was supposed to work, he was granted 45 minutes to attend religious services.
So I am now going to ask the minister whether he intends to take steps to grant Montreal postal employees the same privileges as are enjoyed by others, and to see that the postmaster of Montreal follows the same policy as is followed everywhere else.

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have
already explained what is provided by regulations in this regard, and I can assure the house that no postal employee will be prevented by his work from attending religious services. Again I say that never has the Civil Service Commission authorized, as the hon. member contends, that a period of 45 minutes be taken off the eight working hours of an employee to enable him to attend religious services.
There has always been a rule, at least so I am told, whereby the employees could take that time off, but it was not to be taken off their eight hour day, and that is the rule applying to all postal employees, as well as to those of every other federal department from coast to coast.
I have insisted that this regulation be observed in Montreal and that each employee should have the opportunity of attending religious services if he so wishes, under the circumstances I have mentioned. Since such regulation is established by the civil service commission, I do not have the authority to establish the so-called tradition, to which the hon. member referred a moment ago, but I certainly have the authority to see that the regulation as established is observed. That, I have done.

Then, judging from the statement the hon. minister made in answer to my own, from now on the postal employees of Montreal, on Sundays and days of obligation, will be permitted to disregard the orders of the postmaster, Mr. Rene Boileau, and take, from their eight working hours, the said three quarters of an hour to attend religious services. Is it what the hon. minister has just said?

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Listen, I cannot state it more clearly, and I suggest that the hon. member read my remarks. I have nothing further to add. It is quite clear. I have explained What the civil service commission regulation provided in this regard.

I must inform you that if you again fail in your next examination or do not show up, steps will be taken to reduce your salary further at your next increase date or, if you have reached your maximum salary, at the date where you would have received such an increase.
Signed V. M. Chalin for Rene Boileau, Postmaster.
That is how the department deals with an employee of 35 years standing. He is required, after 35 years of loyal service, to pass, under the threat of a reduction in the salary he has earned for 35 years, an examination which he was able to write successfully 35 years before but which he is no longer in a position to pass with the same facility. He has to take other examinations; I have said and I repeat, Mr. Chairman, that this is foolish, ridiculous and simply leads to hardship toward devoted servants of the people. I suppose that steps should be taken, and will be taken I hope, to decide about the qualifications of employees when they pass their examinations but, for goodness sake, I wish the department would leave them alone for the rest of the time when they serve the state faithfully.
As proof of what I have said, Mr. Chairman, I have here some instructions cpming from Ottawa and dated July 1, 1956. They are called Operation Directives, No. 16 amended. They are sent to all Headquarters Directors, Regional Directors-

I have known many people who have attended universities. When they got out of university, after passing their examinations, they were considered to be qualified lawyers, doctors or qualified in any other profession, and they did not have to pass examinations every year to find out whether they were still competent. We do not see any of these things in any other department of government. Right now we have to consider the fact that in one department, the Post Office Department, this is going on. I say that this should be stopped because a man with 30 years' or 35 years' service cannot be as good as he was 35 years previously when he passed his examination.
(Translation):
I repeat, Mr. Chairman, that, in my opinion, it is sheer cruelty towards postal employees to force them, under threat of a reduction in their salary or of dismissal, to take yearly examinations.
Those are the few comments I had to make, Mr. Chairman, I thank the hon. minister for the assurance he has given us a few moments ago to the effect that the situation which has existed in Montreal for a very long time will continue; I hope that he will take in very serious consideration, in the best interests of his department and of those who for many years have served it faithfully, the few observations which I have just submitted to the house.

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would like to underline only one of my hon. friend's statements. He referred again to the situation in the Montreal central post office as regards attendance at religious services. He should read again the remarks I made when I explained exactly what the regulation was and gave him the assurance that this regulation would be observed.
According to the hon. member, I said that we would come back to the situation prevailing previously. I stated that every post office employee would have a certain time allowed to attend religious services in accordance with the civil service regulation.
Does that mean, Mr. Chairman,-

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I do not propose to pursue that discussion any further. I have stated the situation quite clearly and I have nothing to add.

In order to make all that definitely clear once again, I should like the minister to tell us whether the forty-five minutes to which we both referred would be taken on the eight hours to be worked by the post office employee on Sunday or feast days of obligation.

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: No. Here is what I said exactly. The employee has been allowed 45 minutes to attend mass or any other religious service. However, I did say that he had to fill in his eight hours work just the same.

That is quite ridiculous. The minister's statement does not stand up. It is impossible to give an employee permission to do what he wants outside his working hours. That is his exclusive privilege, whether it be before or after his working hours. I said "during his working hours." If such is the minister's statement, it means that there is nothing changed in the instructions given by the Post Office Department in Montreal and which the minister himself seems to confirm here this afternoon. It means that, from now on post office employees in Montreal, who were entitled to and granted three quarters of an hour of their working time to attend religious services on Sundays and feast days of obligation will no longer have that privilege following the minister's statement.

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: I wonder if it happens sometimes that the hon. member can interpret anyone's words properly. What I said was, and I repeat it, that post office employees in Montreal, like those of all other post offices, are allowed to interrupt their work in order to attend religious services, on the condition that they come back and fill in the time they were allowed. That has always been the rule and that will continue to be the rule of the Post Office Department as long as I am in charge of it. That is a regulation which will be applied to all employees of the department whatever their religious denomination.

Mr. Chairman, I thank the minister for being a little more precise than he had been and I conclude that from now on post office employees in Montreal will be permitted to take the time necessary to attend religious services provided at the end of their day's work they put in the time taken for religious services.

Mr. Chairman, I do not know whether the members from Quebec city have the advantage of the same regulations as we
Supply-Post Office
have in Montreal concerning religious service hours, but I should like to point out to the hon. member that in Montreal we have masses at five o'clock and six o'clock in the morning. Moreover, we also have masses at seven o'clock and eight o'clock at night. Therefore, employees of the Post Office Department do not have to ask permission; they can attend mass at a time convenient to them. The hon. member should let us worry about what concerns Montreal and should concern himself with his own city of Quebec.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for St. Henry (Mr. Bonnier), whom I have seen rise for the first time since I have sat in this house, just made a discovery. He imformed us that masses were being said in Montreal beginning at five o'clock in the morning and also in the evening. It is the same in other cities of the province of Quebec and there is nothing new in that.
Just now, we are considering the position of post office employees in Montreal. We are here to represent those who work in the various departments of the federal government and what I said about the post office employees of Montreal applies also to the electors I have the honour to represent and all those who work for the federal government.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to ask a question of the hon. member for Quebec West.
Go ahead.

Mr. Chairman, I prefer my parish priest's interpretation and that of the archibishop's to that of the hon. member for

Cochrane, and I think he is wrong when he says-
Oh no.
-that the fact of working on a feast day of obligation relieves us of the duty of attending religious services.
That is not what he said.

At any rate, let us understand each other. Whenever I have to seek information on religious matters, I shall try to get it from the religious authorities or from my parish priest, instead of listening to rather fanciful explanations of the hon. member for Cochrane.
What a confused mind!
Mr. Chairman,- (applause).

I am informed that the general turnover throughout Canada is approximately 11.3 per cent. It is higher both in Vancouver and in Toronto as I mentioned the other day in answer to a question. In Vancouver it is 17.2 per cent and in Toronto 19.1.
